title: Spin a hard-boiled egg fast enough and it stands up on its end

cover.alt: A brown egg spinning on its side on a white table, slightly blurred, as a hand pulls away. Another egg sits in an egg tray to the left.

body: Give a hard-boiled egg lying on a table a quick, hard spin and it rises onto one end, lifting its centre of gravity, though nothing seems to push it up. In 2002 Keith Moffatt and Yutaka Shimomura explained why in *Nature*: the spinning egg slips slightly against the table, and that friction acts like a gyroscope, turning some of the spin energy into height. It only works on a surface that is neither too slippery nor too sticky. A raw egg stays flat, because its liquid insides lag behind the shell and soak up the energy.

slides.alt: A hand sets a brown hard-boiled egg spinning on its side on a white table. Within a second the egg rises and spins upright on one end, wobbling, then tips back onto its side and keeps turning.
slides.caption: A hard-boiled egg is flicked into a spin on its side. Moments later it is spinning upright on one end, before slowing and tipping back down.
slides.music: “Monkeys Spinning Monkeys” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.question: About how many turns per second must the egg make before it will rise onto its end?
slides.explanation: About ten revolutions per second, which a firm flick of the wrist can manage.

steps.label: The egg spins fast on its side
It slips slightly against the table
Friction tips its spin axis upwards
Spin energy lifts it onto one end

left.label: Hard-boiled
left.text: Shell and insides turn as one solid body, so friction can trade spin for height and the egg stands up.

right.label: Raw
right.text: The liquid inside lags behind the shell, dragging on it and wasting the spin energy, so the egg stays flat.

slides.heading: Solved in time for Easter
slides.text: Cambridge mathematician Keith Moffatt and physicist Yutaka Shimomura spent about six months of their spare time on the puzzle. Their answer appeared in *Nature* in March 2002. In effect, the egg pays for its rise with some of its spin.

slides.question: Where does the energy to lift the egg's centre of gravity come from?
slides.explanation: Friction with the table converts part of the egg's spin energy into height, so it spins a little slower as it rises.
